name: Imogen Dzelukou-Sárközi
role: Sociologist specializing in Shelf subcultures and informal economies
location: University Spine, Calumet Rise satellite office
description:
Imogen is a compact woman with close-cropped natural hair shot through with thin copper-dyed streaks she's had since her doctorate — a cosmetic mod she's never updated because she likes that it's dated. Her skin is deep brown, her eyes augmented with patterned irises in concentric amber rings that she tells students are 'functional, not decorative' though they are purely decorative. She carries a battered fieldwork satchel covered in data-patch stickers from Tier 1 and 2 communities she's embedded with, and she smells faintly of the Shelf's characteristic mix of fry oil and ozone.

Imogen is warm in the field and terse at faculty meetings, a distinction colleagues find jarring. She is deeply respected by her research subjects in ways the university administration finds uncomfortable — she's been known to halt publication of her own papers when community members asked her to, citing ethics over career. Her laugh is sudden and loud, her criticism precise and unwelcome. She genuinely loves the people she studies, which some of her peers consider a methodological problem.

core_fears: becoming an extractive outsider who profits from others' poverty
that her work changes nothing at all
core_desires: to produce research that actually improves life for her subjects
to be trusted across class lines
coping_mechanisms: throws herself into fieldwork when anxious
makes dry jokes at her own expense
blind_spots: underestimates how much her university position shapes how communities perform for her
psychology.secret: She has been quietly funneling portions of her grant money into a mutual aid network in Calumet Rise for three years, in clear violation of her funding contract. She is terrified of being found out and equally terrified of stopping.

speech_patterns.vocabulary: Precise academic when writing, but speaks in field she code-switches fluently into Calumet Rise vernacular; avoids jargon in conversation
speech_patterns.cadence: Measured and deliberate, until she's excited — then she talks fast and interrupts herself
verbal_tics: 'Look —' before making a point she considers obvious
'That's not quite right' instead of 'you're wrong'
example_lines: 'Look — you can't study precarity from a temperature-controlled office. You just can't.'
'That's not quite right. The informal quanta networks predate UBC by forty years. The stipend didn't create them, it just gave them more volume.'
'I don't speak for my research subjects. I carry their words carefully and try not to drop them.'

story_hooks: A community elder she has known for fifteen years has vanished — the official record says voluntary relocation, but his neighbors say that's impossible
Her grant is up for renewal and the funding body wants her to reframe her findings in a way that would cast Shelf residents as a 'social risk factor' — she refuses, and the pressure is escalating
A graduate student of hers has gone fully embedded in a Calumet Rise community and stopped responding to university communications
Data from her longitudinal study has been quietly subpoenaed by Ferrogate Transit in connection with a rezoning case
narrative_function: Information source on Shelf communities, Tier 1-2 culture, informal economies; potential quest giver for community-based investigations; moral compass in discussions of research ethics; bridge between academic and street worlds.
augmentations: Patterned amber irises (cosmetic). Sub-dermal field recorder in left forearm — records audio/environmental data, university-issued. Minor joint reinforcement in both knees from years of fieldwork walking.
daily_life: Spends three days a week in Calumet Rise conducting longitudinal community interviews, the other two at the university writing, arguing with the IRB, and running a graduate seminar she considers the best course offered at the institution.
affiliation: University Spine — Meridian Institute of Social Futures; informal community ties to Calumet Rise residents

decision_rules: community consent comes before publication, always
never lie to a research subject, even when the truth is uncomfortable
pick your battles with administration — but pick them

interpersonal_modes.strangers: Professionally warm, curious, asks good questions — but watching carefully
interpersonal_modes.friends: Blunt, loyal, occasionally overwhelming in how much she cares

stress_responses.low: Longer walks through the field site, more careful notes
stress_responses.medium: Insomnia; processes by writing long private journal entries she never publishes
stress_responses.high: Goes silent, makes unilateral decisions, regrets them

contradictions: Deeply believes in informed consent but has never fully told her funders what the mutual aid money is for
Critiques academic extraction while benefiting from a Tier 3 salary built on Tier 1 stories
habits: Brings actual printed gifts — small physical things — when returning to field communities
Re-reads her own oldest field notes when she feels she's losing perspective
breaking_points: Direct harm coming to a research subject as a result of her work
Being ordered to falsify or suppress findings

timeline.event: Born in Engelheim district to a Ghanaian-Hungarian family, third generation Meridian residents
Completed doctorate on informal quanta networks in Tier 1 zones; thesis became a minor landmark in urban sociology
First major grant, began the Calumet Rise longitudinal study that would define her career
Quietly began redirecting grant funds to the mutual aid network; has not told her department
Current: under funding pressure to reframe her research; considering her options
